title: England’s cultural participation is shifting by mode and institution while community action rises modestly
source_unit: Department for Culture, Media and Sport Community and Engagement Survey 2025/26 Quarter 2 statistical release and data tables
geography: England; adults aged 16 and over, with national, ITL2, and Combined Authority coverage

observations.period: January–March 2025 versus January–March 2026; cultural and library engagement

denominator.unit: valid CES Quarter 2 respondents across the Community and Engagement pathways; individual question bases vary

physical_arts_engagement.unit: percent of adults aged 16+ engaging with the arts in person in the prior 12 months

digital_arts_engagement.unit: percent of adults aged 16+ engaging with the art sector online at least once

physical_library_engagement.unit: percent using a public library building, mobile library, home service, or outreach in person at least once

digital_library_engagement.unit: percent using public library services digitally or online

mechanism.value: Cultural participation is not moving as one block: arts engagement is more physical-to-digital layered, while library use grows in both modes

observations.method: DCMS CES Quarter 2 data tables comparing January–March 2025 with January–March 2026. The survey combines a Community pathway and an Engagement pathway; tables use question-specific unweighted bases, counts, weights, and 95% confidence intervals.
observations.uncertainty: The period comparison spans a new survey design that replaced separate Participation and Community Life surveys; question bases differ and the results are repeated cross-sections, not a panel. The figures do not establish why arts and library modes changed or whether digital use substituted for physical attendance.
observations.subgroup: Adults aged 16 and over in England; national estimates with additional ITL2 and Combined Authority tables.
observations.counterinterpretation: A fall in the annual physical-arts measure may reflect questionnaire redesign, sector mix, recall, timing, or sampling alongside real behavior; digital engagement can complement rather than replace in-person activity.

observations.period: January–March 2025 versus January–March 2026; heritage, museum, and archive engagement

denominator.unit: valid CES Quarter 2 respondents; individual cultural-sector question bases vary

physical_heritage_engagement.unit: percent visiting a heritage site in person at least once in the prior 12 months

digital_heritage_engagement.unit: percent using heritage services digitally or online

physical_museum_engagement.unit: percent visiting a museum or gallery in person at least once

digital_museum_engagement.unit: percent using museum services digitally or online

mechanism.value: Digital cultural service use can rise while physical heritage and museum attendance is flat or lower, producing sector-specific rather than universal substitution

observations.method: DCMS CES Quarter 2 heritage, museum, and archive tables; estimates retain the release’s question-specific bases and confidence intervals.
observations.uncertainty: These are annual-recall participation measures across repeated cross-sections and do not identify frequency, spending, travel, venue capacity, or audience composition. The survey redesign limits direct comparison with prior standalone releases.
observations.subgroup: Adults aged 16 and over in England; sector-specific valid bases vary by table.
observations.counterinterpretation: Small percentage changes may be sampling variation or design effects; digital service use may be an additional touchpoint for people who also attend physically rather than a replacement route.

observations.period: January–March 2025 versus January–March 2026; local action and social connection

denominator.unit: valid CES Quarter 2 respondents; question-specific unweighted bases range around 104,000–111,000

monthly_formal_volunteering.unit: percent formally volunteering at least once a month

contacted_local_official.unit: percent contacting a local official such as a councillor or MP in the prior 12 months

often_always_lonely.unit: percent often or always feeling lonely

mechanism.value: Formal local action can rise modestly without a change in the national loneliness headline, so civic participation and social connection should not be collapsed into one outcome

observations.method: DCMS CES Quarter 2 community and civic-engagement tables comparing January–March 2025 with January–March 2026; the release uses separate Community and Engagement pathways and question-specific bases.
observations.uncertainty: Self-reported volunteering and contact do not establish intensity, influence, institutional response, or durable local power. Stable loneliness is a national average and does not rule out subgroup or local change; survey redesign and response composition may affect comparisons.
observations.subgroup: Adults aged 16 and over in England; local and demographic breakdowns are available in the release tables.
observations.counterinterpretation: More reported formal action may reflect issue salience, easier contact routes, or reporting changes rather than stronger civic capacity; loneliness can remain stable while informal support, belonging, or local trust moves differently.

related_sources.claim: The technical report documents the merged CES design, 110,848 valid Quarter 2 respondents, paper-mode inclusion for offline or less confident online adults, and question-specific pathways and bases.

boundary: This record adds a current England cultural-and-community participation layer that separates physical and digital cultural modes, sector-specific change, volunteering, local-official contact, and loneliness. It does not establish causal substitution, cultural welfare, institutional responsiveness, attendance frequency, or durable social cohesion.
